name: Deep Shaft Minor

stars.name: Shaft Light
stars.notes: Ancient red dwarf with extreme metallicity from its formation in a metal-rich nebula. Its age has allowed rare radioactive decay products to accumulate in the planetary system.

planets.name: Adit
planets.notes: Tidally locked world with exposed veins of rare actinide compounds on the nightside. Automated extraction targets thorium and other heavy elements.

planets.name: Winze
planets.notes: Dense, geologically quiet world with subsurface deposits of rare lanthanides. Deep bore mining reaches deposits at 40+ kilometer depths.

planets.name: Sump
planets.notes: Frozen outer body with a mantle of water ice over a rocky core. The core contains trace amounts of exotic superheavy elements detectable only by deep drilling.

anomalies.name: The Glow
anomalies.location: Surface of Adit, nightside equatorial region
anomalies.notes: A faint visible luminescence emanating from exposed actinide veins on Adit's nightside. The radiation is measurable but not dangerous at orbital distances. Its spectral signature includes unidentified emission lines.

asteroid_belts.name: Heavy Scatter
asteroid_belts.notes: Thin belt of dense, metal-heavy asteroids containing rare earth elements and trace actinides. Each rock is individually tagged and tracked due to the value of its contents.

stations.name: Deep Shaft Processing Lab
stations.notes: Combined extraction coordination center and analytical laboratory. Rare element samples are processed and cataloged here before shipment to research institutions and industrial buyers.

stations.name: Beacon DSM
stations.notes: Unmanned navigation beacon and communications relay. Guides the infrequent supply ships and ore haulers to the system.

faction_control.notes: Government research agency with exclusive extraction rights. The system's rare element deposits are considered strategically sensitive, limiting commercial access.

history: Identified in 2501 during a deep-space spectroscopic survey that flagged the system's unusual heavy element signatures as warranting investigation.

The Exotic Materials Bureau claimed exclusive rights in 2504 after initial probes confirmed the presence of rare actinides and potential superheavy elements, classifying the system as a restricted research zone.

The Glow phenomenon on Adit was first observed in 2512 and remains unexplained; its unidentified spectral lines have attracted interest from physicists who believe they may indicate the presence of island-of-stability superheavy elements.
description: Deep Shaft Minor is a small, dim system at the edge of the Outer Ferric Expanse, remarkable not for the quantity of its resources but for their rarity. Three worlds circle the ancient red dwarf Shaft Light, whose extreme age and metal-rich origins have produced a planetary system enriched with heavy elements found almost nowhere else in accessible space. The system's name reflects both the deep bore mining required to reach its treasures and its modest physical scale--three small worlds, a thin asteroid belt, and a skeleton crew of specialists.

The Exotic Materials Bureau operates Deep Shaft Minor as a restricted research and extraction zone. The materials recovered here--thorium isotopes, rare lanthanides, and tantalizing traces of superheavy elements--feed cutting-edge research programs and specialized industrial applications. Production volumes are tiny by conventional mining standards but enormously valuable per kilogram. The 120-person crew at the Processing Lab includes as many scientists as miners, and every sample is cataloged with the care of a museum curator handling antiquities.

The Glow on Adit's nightside is the system's enduring mystery. The faint luminescence from exposed actinide veins includes spectral lines that match no known element, leading some physicists to theorize that Shaft Light's ancient protoplanetary disk produced trace quantities of island-of-stability superheavy elements--atoms with atomic numbers above 120 that theory predicts could be metastable over geological timescales. If confirmed, such a discovery would rewrite nuclear physics and make Deep Shaft Minor one of the most scientifically significant locations in known space. The Bureau keeps its findings close, and access remains tightly controlled.
